source.title: [Replication] Conjecture's Sparse Coding in Small Transformers

record.tranche_reason: The authors describe replicating sparse-coding experiments with a custom-trained small transformer and report cross-dictionary MMCS results, using the same kind of dictionary comparison as the earlier work.
record.gate_note: The post reports cross-dictionary feature-similarity results and changes with dictionary size and training time. It does not report whether the inputs activating a coarse feature are partitioned among finer features. The random-vector comparison for neuron-basis sparsity is not a result about the claim.
record.test_reason: The post replicates Sharkey et al.'s cross-dictionary convergence test, the MMCS-with-larger metric, on one small custom transformer. MMCS asks whether a smaller dictionary's features have near-identical counterparts in larger dictionaries. That measures feature persistence and convergence across sizes, not splitting. The post never identifies a coarse feature replaced by several finer features near its direction. It does not test input coverage, hierarchy, absorption, decomposition into combinations, or training objectives. This is a related but different construct, so the findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say they replicated Sharkey and Braun's core results on a 6-layer, 32-dimensional-residual transformer. Many more features than activation dimensions are recovered and recur across dictionary sizes, with bimodal MCS. MMCS rises and then plateaus with size, and grows only slowly with training. The diagonal lines in hyperparameter space were an artefact of dividing L1 by dictionary size. The learned features are not sparse in the neuron basis. Max-activating examples often look interpretable, but this is not yet tested quantitatively.
record.recipe_differences: Applied sparse coding and cross-dictionary cosine comparisons to activations from a custom-trained small transformer. The authors describe replicating the earlier technique; the model and activation setting differ from the toy-model work.
record.method_sensitivity: Dictionary size affects the reported cross-dictionary alignment; MMCS-with-larger rises with additional training, though slowly. The authors also report that dividing the l1-loss term by dictionary size caused diagonal patterns in hyperparameter space and that removing this division changed those patterns.

fits_no_version.finding: Across dictionary sizes, the MCS distribution between dictionaries is bimodal. A set of features recurs near-identically across sizes, and its count grows with size; the rest are near-random, and many are dead.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAEs of different sizes converge on a shared core of features, plus non-convergent, random-like features.

fits_no_version.finding: MMCS-with-larger rises slowly with extra training. The number of features with MCS above 0.9 increases significantly, but full convergence is unclear.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-dictionary feature convergence improves with training time.

record.problems: One small custom-trained transformer is studied. The post gives qualitative descriptions rather than exact MMCS values or feature counts for the comparisons, and it does not test whether high-similarity features partition a coarse feature's inputs.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results identified. The neuron-basis sparsity comparison and interpretability examples do not measure the claim's cross-dictionary splitting behavior.

untested.parts: All parts: no coarse-to-fine replacement, no coverage of inputs, no proximity of child directions to a parent.
All parts: one tiny custom transformer, no open SAE releases.
All parts: neither decomposition of larger latents into combinations nor novel latents in larger SAEs is measured.
Splitting is not examined. The only objective-related finding is that dividing the L1 coefficient by dictionary size caused the diagonal patterns in hyperparameter space.

missing.what: Summary statement that MMCS rises rapidly with dictionary size and then plateaus. This bears on convergence, not on a version.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests' and T1 relation and its V1/V5 support labels are not justified. The original sources here are Anthropic's splitting work and the absorption and canonical-units papers, whereas this post replicates a different metric: convergence across dictionary sizes. The Figure 1 caption refers to a 128-dimensional activation, so layer 2's MLP rather than the residual stream. All results are qualitative, read from figures without stated numbers.

versions.untested_parts: Tests cross-dictionary cosine alignment, but does not show a coarse feature being replaced by several finer features or test whether those features partition the coarse feature's inputs.
The study uses one custom-trained small transformer, not large models or open SAE releases.
Does not test nested feature families or whether they mirror a conceptual hierarchy.
Does not study parent-child firing, absorption, or whether size or sparsity changes fix absorption.

Measures feature similarity and analogues across dictionary sizes, but does not test whether larger latents decompose into combinations of smaller latents or establish that no dictionary size yields a complete atomic set.
Does not test whether splitting is an artifact of the SAE objective on hierarchical inputs or compare with Matryoshka SAEs.

rows.subject: small transformer trained with nanoGPT
rows.size_stated: 6 layers; 32-dimensional residual stream; MLP widths of 128; 4 attention heads with dimension 8
rows.operation_detail: Compared sparse-coding dictionaries of different sizes using MMCS-with-larger.

conditions.value: varied; exact sizes not stated for this comparison

rows.value: Smaller dictionaries had high MMCS-with-larger scores against larger dictionaries; results for larger dictionaries were described as mixed.
rows.note: Reports cross-size similarity, not a partition of a coarse feature's inputs.
rows.check: MMCS-with-larger measures whether small-dictionary features persist in larger dictionaries, not whether coarse features split into finer ones. The text also says the larger-dictionary results are 'mixed'; no values are given.

rows.subject: small transformer trained with nanoGPT
rows.size_stated: 6 layers; 32-dimensional residual stream; MLP widths of 128; 4 attention heads with dimension 8
rows.operation_detail: Compared features in the 512 dictionary with features in larger dictionaries using MCS.
rows.measure: Distribution of maximum cosine similarity (MCS) to features in larger dictionaries
rows.value: Most features were described as nearly identical to features consistently found by larger dictionaries.
rows.note: The text describes a high-similarity group and a lower-similarity peak around 0.25–0.4.
rows.check: Near-identical features across sizes show convergence or stability, not splitting. High MCS to one larger feature, if anything, indicates no split. No numbers are given.

rows.subject: small transformer trained with nanoGPT
rows.size_stated: 6 layers; 32-dimensional residual stream; MLP widths of 128; 4 attention heads with dimension 8
rows.operation_detail: Compared features in the 2048 dictionary with features in the 4096 dictionary using MCS.
rows.measure: Whether features had a similar analogue in the larger dictionary
rows.value: The majority of 2048-dictionary features had no analogue in the 4096 dictionary; many of those features were never used.
rows.note: No-analogue features are relevant to the novel-latent part of V5, but the study does not test combinations of smaller latents.
rows.check: The direction is reversed relative to V5: these are 2048-dictionary features lacking a 4096 analogue, not novel latents in the larger SAE. Many are 'never used' (dead), and their MCS peak matches random vectors, so they are untrained directions rather than novel features.

rows.subject: small transformer trained with nanoGPT
rows.size_stated: 6 layers; 32-dimensional residual stream; MLP widths of 128; 4 attention heads with dimension 8
rows.operation_detail: Compared the number of highly similar features across dictionary sizes using MCS.
rows.measure: Number of highly similar features across dictionaries
rows.value: The number of highly similar features at size 2048 was larger than at size 512.
rows.note: The text does not give the counts.
rows.check: The count of highly similar (convergent) features grows with dictionary size. This bears on convergence, not on splitting or on decomposition into combinations of smaller latents. No counts are given.

rows.note: The authors describe the evidence for eventual convergence as mixed.
rows.check: This is a training-time convergence result and does not bear on dictionary-size splitting. 'partial' is not a meaningful state against V1.

rows.check: The rise in the count of features above 0.9 MCS during training is a convergence measure, not splitting. No counts are given.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Smaller dictionaries had high MMCS-with-larger scores and most 512-dictionary features were described as nearly identical to features found by larger dictionaries (R1, R2). This supports cross-size directional correspondence, not input partitioning.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The larger-dictionary comparisons were mixed, and MMCS rose slowly with training without clear full convergence (R3, R5). The study does not establish the complete split-and-cover pattern.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Most features in the 2048 dictionary reportedly had no analogue in the 4096 dictionary, consistent with the novel-latent part of V5; the number of highly similar features also grew with dictionary size (R3, R4).
